question.prompt: In Coinland, there are three types of coins, each worth \(6,\) \(10,\) and \(15.\) What is the sum of the digits of the maximum amount of money that is impossible to have?

solutions.title: Build six consecutive amounts
solutions.explanation:
Once six consecutive integer amounts are obtainable, adding \(6\)-coins makes every larger integer amount obtainable as well. We therefore look for such a block just above a candidate impossible amount.

The following six amounts can all be made:

| Amount | Coin combination |
|---:|---|
| \(30\) | \(5\cdot6\) |
| \(31\) | \(6+10+15\) |
| \(32\) | \(2\cdot6+2\cdot10\) |
| \(33\) | \(3\cdot6+15\) |
| \(34\) | \(4\cdot6+10\) |
| \(35\) | \(2\cdot10+15\) |

For any integer amount above \(35\), repeatedly subtract \(6\) until the result lies between \(30\) and \(35\). Reversing these subtractions adds \(6\)-coins to a combination in the table. Thus every integer amount at least \(30\) is obtainable.

Now consider \(29\). Coins worth \(6\) and \(10\) contribute an even total, so an odd number of \(15\)-coins would be necessary. Since two \(15\)-coins already exceed \(29\), exactly one would be required, leaving \(14\).

To make \(14\) using \(6\)- and \(10\)-coins, there could be zero or one \(10\)-coin. These cases leave \(14\) or \(4\), respectively, neither of which is a nonnegative multiple of \(6\). Therefore \(29\) is impossible.

The largest impossible amount is consequently \(29\), and its digit sum is
\[
\boxed{2+9=11},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

solutions.title: Find the first amount in each remainder
solutions.explanation:
Adding a \(6\)-coin preserves the remainder upon division by \(6\). Finding the smallest obtainable amount for each remainder will therefore locate every possible gap.

Write an obtainable amount as
\[
n=6a+10b+15c,
\]
where \(a,b,c\) are nonnegative integers counting the three coin types.

In the smallest obtainable amount for a fixed remainder modulo \(6\), we must have \(a=0\), since otherwise we could remove a \(6\)-coin and get a smaller amount with the same remainder. Also, \(b\le2\): removing three \(10\)-coins subtracts \(30\), again preserving the remainder. Similarly, \(c\le1\), since two \(15\)-coins could be removed.

Thus each minimum must occur among the six combinations with
\[
a=0,\qquad b\in\{0,1,2\},\qquad c\in\{0,1\}.
\]
These combinations give all six different remainders:

| Remainder modulo \(6\) | Smallest obtainable amount \(m\) | Largest nonnegative impossible amount in that remainder |
|---:|---|---:|
| \(0\) | \(0\), using no coins | none |
| \(1\) | \(25=10+15\) | \(19\) |
| \(2\) | \(20=2\cdot10\) | \(14\) |
| \(3\) | \(15\) | \(9\) |
| \(4\) | \(10\) | \(4\) |
| \(5\) | \(35=2\cdot10+15\) | \(29\) |

The restrictions on \(a,b,c\) prove that these amounts are minimal. For each row, every amount with that remainder at least \(m\) is obtainable by adding \(6\)-coins. Every smaller amount in that remainder is impossible, so the last impossible one is \(m-6\). For remainder \(0\), all nonnegative multiples of \(6\) are obtainable.

The largest gap in the table is \(29\). Hence the requested digit sum is
\[
\boxed{2+9=11},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
